title: Should we open a second fulfillment center? Decision architecture
caption: Howard-Matheson influence diagram for a direct-to-consumer brand's 18-month capacity decision. Decisions are rectangles, uncertainties ovals, the deterministic margin node a rounded rectangle, and 24-month net contribution the value node.

nodes.label: Site & lease (Q3)
nodes.description: Whether and where to sign an 18-month lease on a second fulfillment center: East hub, West hub, or defer.

nodes.label: Pick & pack capacity (Q1 next yr)
nodes.description: After the holiday peak is observed, how many automated pick lines to staff at the chosen site.

nodes.label: Holiday demand surge
nodes.description: Peak-season order volume vs. forecast: below, on, or above plan.

nodes.label: Regional split (East vs West)
nodes.description: Share of orders shipping to each coast, which determines transit savings from a second hub.

nodes.label: Carrier rate change
nodes.description: Parcel-carrier contract repricing at renewal: cut, flat, or surcharge.

nodes.label: Labor availability at site
nodes.description: Whether the local labor market fills the staffed pick lines at planned wage.

nodes.label: Per-order fulfillment margin
nodes.description: Computed margin per order given site, staffed lines, regional split, and carrier rate.

nodes.label: 24-month net contribution
nodes.description: Total contribution over the lease horizon: order margin times volume, less lease and automation cost.

arcs.note: Trailing regional shipping mix is known before the site is chosen.
Site is fixed before capacity is staffed (no-forgetting).
Holiday surge is observed before the capacity decision.
Chosen site sets baseline handling cost.
Staffed pick lines set throughput and labor cost.
Regional split drives transit savings from the second hub.
Carrier rate scales parcel cost per order.
Labor shortfall degrades realized throughput vs. staffed plan.
Lease commitment is a fixed cost over the horizon.
Automation capex is a fixed cost over the horizon.

semantic_description.level_1_elemental: Howard-Matheson influence diagram with eight nodes: two rectangle decision nodes (site & lease D1, pick-pack capacity D2), four oval chance nodes (holiday demand, regional split, carrier rate, labor availability), one rounded-rectangle deterministic node (per-order margin), and one hexagonal value node (24-month net contribution). Dashed arcs are informational (what is known at each decision); solid arcs are functional or relevance influences.
semantic_description.level_2_statistical: Twelve arcs. The value node V1 has three functional parents (per-order margin T1, holiday demand C1, site D1) plus D2; the deterministic margin node T1 has five parents (D1, D2, regional split C2, carrier rate C3, labor C4). Temporal order C2 < D1 < C1 < D2 gives two sequential decisions with three pre-decision observations.
semantic_description.level_3_perceptual: Information flows left to right toward a single value node on the right. The diagram reads as a two-stage decision: choose the site after seeing the regional shipping mix, then size capacity after the holiday surge is observed. All uncertainty funnels through the per-order margin node, while demand volume and the two fixed-cost commitments reach the value node directly.
semantic_description.level_4_contextual: Separating the irreversible lease (D1) from the deferrable, information-richer capacity decision (D2) is the core of the architecture: the option value lives in waiting to staff lines until peak demand is observed.
semantic_description.short_alt: Influence diagram: two decisions (site, capacity) feed per-order margin and 24-month net contribution under demand and cost uncertainty.
